theory.intro: Congruent figures are identical: they have exactly the same shape and the same size. If a translation (slide), a reflection (flip) or a rotation (turn) can move one figure exactly on top of another, the two figures are congruent.
facts: Translations, reflections and rotations do not change side lengths or angles, so the image is always congruent to the original.
In congruent figures, corresponding (matching) sides are equal and corresponding angles are equal.
Matching marks show the correspondence: sides with the same number of tick marks are equal, and angles with the same mark are equal.
Two circles are congruent exactly when their radii are equal.
Figures with the same shape but different sizes are **not** congruent.
steps: Decide whether a translation, reflection or rotation moves one figure exactly onto the other: slid → translation, back-to-front → reflection, turned → rotation.
Match each vertex of the original with its image, using the transformation or the matching marks.
Read off the corresponding sides and angles from the matched vertices.

foundation.solution_text:
The image is the same way up and the same way around — $\triangle ABC$ has slid across without turning or flipping.
The transformation is a translation.

The image is back-to-front compared with the original — it has been flipped over the dashed mirror line.
The transformation is a reflection.

The image has been turned to point in a different direction, but it is not back-to-front.
The transformation is a rotation.

Both rectangles are $8$ m by $4$ m, so all matching sides and all matching angles are equal.
A translation moves one exactly onto the other, so the rectangles are congruent.

$B$ is the vertex where the double-tick side meets the single-tick side.
In $\triangle LMN$ the double-tick side $MN$ meets the single-tick side $NL$ at $N$.
$B$ corresponds to $N$.

The reflection matches $A \leftrightarrow F$, $B \leftrightarrow E$, $C \leftrightarrow H$ and $D \leftrightarrow G$.
Side $AD$ corresponds to side $FG$.

$\angle B$ carries the double arc.
In $\triangle XYZ$ the double arc is at $Y$.
$\angle B$ corresponds to $\angle Y$.

Two circles are congruent exactly when their radii are equal.
Both radii are $4$ cm, so the circles are congruent.

development.solution_text:
The rectangles have the same shape, but the matching sides are $8$ cm and $12$ cm, which are not equal.
No translation, reflection or rotation can move one exactly onto the other, so the rectangles are not congruent.

Following each vertex through the quarter turn: the shortest side $AB$ maps onto $PQ$ and the longest side $BC$ maps onto $QR$.
$A \leftrightarrow P$, $B \leftrightarrow Q$ and $C \leftrightarrow R$.

Side $TU$ carries the double tick.
In $\triangle XYZ$ the double tick is on side $YZ$.
$TU$ corresponds to $YZ$.

$\angle D$ carries the double arc.
In $EFGH$ the double arc is at $H$.
$\angle D$ corresponds to $\angle H$.

The radius of circle $P$ is $10 \div 2 = 5$ cm.
The radii are equal, so the circles are congruent.

The image is back-to-front: the tall arm of the figure has swapped from the left side to the right side.
The transformation is a reflection.

mastery.solution_text:
Congruent figures need equal matching angles as well as equal matching sides.
The square's angles are all $90^{\circ}$, but the rhombus's angles are not, so no translation, reflection or rotation can move one shape exactly onto the other.
Kai is not correct — the shapes are not congruent.

$A$ is the vertex where the single-tick side meets the unmarked side.
In $WXYZ$ the single-tick side $WX$ meets the unmarked side $ZW$ at $W$.
$A$ corresponds to $W$.

Every translation, reflection and rotation leaves side lengths and angles unchanged, so any sequence of them also leaves the size and shape unchanged.
Zara is not correct — the figures are congruent.
